design_detail: Secondary, pooled analysis by the original Johns Hopkins team of two double-blind laboratory studies of psilocybin in hallucinogen-naive healthy volunteers. Study 1 (Griffiths et al., 2006): psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg in one session and methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg (active control) in the other one or two. Study 2 (Griffiths et al., 2011): psilocybin 5, 10, 20 and 30 mg/70 kg in ascending or descending order (50% random assignment) with a placebo session inserted quasi-randomly (study conditions). 52 participants (35 and 17) completed the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised at screening, 1-2 months after each session and about 14 months after the last session (follow-up a mean of 16 months after the high-dose session). The main analysis is a within-person change in personality from screening to 1-2 months after the 30 mg/70 kg session (repeated-measures ANOVA), not a contrast between randomized conditions; the only comparison with sessions without high-dose psilocybin is a separate test of change after the first session in the 30 participants whose first session was placebo, methylphenidate or 5 mg/70 kg. Participants were then split by whether they met an a priori criterion for a 'complete mystical experience' (at least 60% on each of six SOCQ subscales) during the high-dose session, a grouping by what happened in the session, not by randomization (pp. 1454-1456). Filed as crossover-rct because the parent studies are double-blind within-person trials; appraised with RoB 2 as the batch brief directs.
can_establish: That in 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, mostly spiritually active volunteers who took a high dose of psilocybin with extensive preparation and support, self-rated Openness was on average 2.8 T-score points higher 1-2 months later while the other four personality domains did not change detectably, and that the rise was concentrated in the 30 who reported a 'complete mystical experience'.
cannot_establish: That psilocybin caused the change (personality change was not compared between randomized conditions, so time, retesting, expectation and the preparation and contact with staff are not controlled); that the mystical experience caused it (the experience was not assigned, so whatever made someone have one, such as expectations or readiness to report change, could also drive the self-ratings); that behaviour changed (self-report questionnaires only, no observer ratings in this paper); or how far it applies to people who are not well-educated, spiritually active volunteers with high baseline Openness, or to use outside a laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Community volunteers recruited by flyers announcing a study of states of consciousness brought about by psilocybin, described as a naturally occurring substance used sacramentally in some cultures; a scripted telephone screen (passed by about 20% of those screened), then in-person screening of medical and psychiatric health; unpaid; participants generally reported being motivated by curiosity about psilocybin and the opportunity for extensive self-reflection (Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, p. 1454).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Criteria similar across the two studies and described in the original reports (not here); Study 2 allowed limited prior hallucinogen experience. The one Study 2 participant with lifetime psilocybin use was excluded from this analysis, and one Study 1 participant with incomplete personality data; all 52 analysed were hallucinogen-naive (p. 1454).
sample.demographics: Study 1: mean age 46 (range 24-64), 14 men and 21 women; Study 2: mean age 46 (29-62), 8 men and 9 women (Table 1, p. 1455). 54% had postgraduate degrees and 90% regularly took part in religious services, discussion groups, prayer or meditation (p. 1454). Screening NEO T scores (population mean 50, SD 10), Study 1 and Study 2: Openness 65.4 and 62.7, Neuroticism 41.8 and 46.1, Extroversion 55.3 and 52.1, Agreeableness 55.7 and 55.1, Conscientiousness 51.0 and 51.7; no study differences at screening (p > 0.10) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Post-test: 52 of 52 analysed. Follow-up: 51; the 'no complete mystical experience' group has 21 at follow-up against 22 at post-test, and the missing participant is not described (p. 1457). Two participants of the parent studies were excluded before analysis for the reasons above.
sample.selection_effects: Highly selected: unpaid volunteers drawn by a psilocybin study framed around sacramental use, about 80% of telephone-screened people not passing, mostly highly educated and spiritually active, with baseline Openness about 1.3 to 1.5 population SDs above the norm. The authors suggest that spiritually active people may be particularly sensitive to the mystical-type effects that predicted the Openness increase (p. 1459). Expectations of personal change are likely in such a group and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Drug, dose and session order set by the parent studies' double-blind protocols: participants were told they would receive a 'moderate or high dose' of psilocybin in one session, but neither they nor the monitors knew which (p. 1455). Mystical-type experience rated about 7 hours after capsule intake with the 43 mystical items of the States of Consciousness Questionnaire (SOCQ; six subscales expressed as percentage of maximum), plus the session version of the Hood Mysticism Scale and the APZ scales OSE ('oceanic boundlessness'), VUS ('visionary restructuralization') and AIA ('dread of ego dissolution') (pp. 1455-1456).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral psilocybin capsules at 30 mg/70 kg body weight in the analysed high-dose session; methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg in Study 1 control sessions; psilocybin 5, 10 and 20 mg/70 kg and a placebo session in Study 2; 2 to 5 sessions of 8 hours at least 3 weeks apart; at least 8 hours of meetings with session monitors before the first session; during sessions participants lay on a couch with an eye mask and headphones playing music and focused on inner experience (p. 1455).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported in this paper (drug use outside the studies is not described; the parent studies' criteria apply).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. Personality after the high-dose session was always measured within 1-2 months of it and before any later session (p. 1456).

comparison.controls: No concurrent control for the main change score: each person's screening score is the reference. In a separate within-group test, the 30 participants whose first session was placebo, methylphenidate or psilocybin 5 mg/70 kg showed no change in Openness after that session (F(1, 29) = 0.52, p = 0.48); the paper does not test this change against the change after the high-dose session (p. 1456). The mystical-experience comparison sets the 30 people who met the criterion against the 22 who did not, a non-randomized split.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Screening Openness and its facets did not differ between the mystical-experience groups (p > 0.10, Figure 2 legend, p. 1458), and the SOCQ mystical score did not correlate with screening Openness (r = 0.12, p = 0.41) (p. 1456).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations of change, suggestibility and absorption were not reported; spiritual practice was described but not analysed; personality trajectories before screening are unknown.

outcomes.instruments: NEO Personality Inventory-Revised, computer version, 240 items rated on a 5-point scale; five domains with six facets each; raw scores converted to T scores with the combined-sex norms of the manual; given at screening, 1-2 months after each session and about 14 months after the last session (Methods › Measures, p. 1455).
outcomes.validity_norms: The NEO PI-R is a widely used normed instrument. The SOCQ mystical items have no published psychometric validation; the authors cite unpublished factor data from their laboratory (p. 1459).
outcomes.operationalization: Personality change = difference in T score from screening to post-test (1-2 months after the high-dose session) or to follow-up (mean 16 months). 'Complete mystical experience' = at least 60% of the maximum on each of six SOCQ subscales, an a priori criterion carried over from the group's earlier work (pp. 1455-1456).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five domains tested at post-test (Openness was the stated hypothesis), six Openness facets, five session-day questionnaire correlations (Pearson and Spearman) and four stepwise regressions, all at p < 0.05 (editors' count). Against a Bonferroni threshold of 0.01 for five domains, the whole-sample Openness change (p = 0.023) would not pass (editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-report questionnaires, completed 1-2 months after a session whose high dose participants could recognise, so self-raters were probably not blind to having had the high dose by then.

analysis.effect_sizes: Openness, all 52, screening to post-test: +2.8 T points, F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023, partial eta squared 0.10 (p. 1456); editors' calculation: within-person standardized change dz about 0.32. Other domains: Neuroticism -0.5 (F(1, 51) = 0.24, p = 0.62), Extroversion +0.8 (p = 0.38), Agreeableness +1.7 (F = 2.31, printed p = 0.16), Conscientiousness -0.9 (p = 0.28); test-retest correlations 0.61-0.84 (p. 1456). SOCQ mystical score and Openness change: r = 0.42, p = 0.002, n = 52 (editors' 95% CI about 0.17 to 0.62, Fisher z); Spearman 0.47. Openness change also correlated with the Mysticism Scale (r = 0.33), OSE (0.44), VUS (0.41) and AIA (0.31); the SOCQ added R-squared 0.042 to 0.12 over each (pp. 1456-1457). Complete vs no complete mystical experience: time by group F(1, 50) = 9.32, p = 0.004, partial eta squared 0.16; change +5.7 (t(29) = 3.44, p = 0.002; editors' dz about 0.63) vs -1.2 (t(21) = 0.87, p = 0.39) (p. 1457). Follow-up, complete group: +4.2 vs screening, F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050 (editors' calculation 0.0503), partial eta squared 0.13; no-complete group: -0.3, p = 0.86 (p. 1457). Editors' calculation from the subgroup means: about +2.3 T points for all 51 at follow-up, a figure the paper neither reports nor tests.
analysis.covariates: None in the ANOVAs. The stepwise regressions entered screening Openness, then one other session-day questionnaire, then the SOCQ (p. 1456).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned in this paper; the hypothesis that mystical experiences would lead to enduring increases in Openness is stated in the Introduction (p. 1454). The registration of the parent studies is not stated here.
analysis.selective_reporting: The whole-sample Openness change at follow-up is not reported, only the two mystical-experience subgroups. The change after the high-dose session is not tested against the change after control sessions. Facet results are given as p values and a figure only.
analysis.power: No power calculation; the authors pooled the two studies to gain statistical power (p. 1456).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Self-rated Openness was on average 2.8 T points (about a third of a population SD) higher 1-2 months after a high-dose psilocybin session in 52 highly selected volunteers; the other four domains did not change detectably. The rise was in the 30 who reported a 'complete mystical experience' (+5.7) and not in the other 22 (-1.2); individual changes ranged widely (about -12 to +36 in Figure 1). At about 16 months the mystical-experience group was 4.2 points above screening at p = 0.0503 and the others 0.3 below; the whole sample's follow-up change is not reported. No behavioural or observer measure of personality was included.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says mystical experiences 'lead to increases' in Openness, a causal verb for an experience that was not assigned. The abstract says Openness remained significantly higher than baseline more than a year later in those with mystical experiences (p. 1453), on a result at p = 0.050. The Discussion calls this the first study to demonstrate personality change in healthy adults after an experimentally manipulated discrete event, and the conclusion says the high dose 'produced increases in Openness' (pp. 1458, 1460), although the change was measured against each person's own screening score, not against a randomized control condition. The comparison with normal ageing (about 1 T point per decade) and with antidepressant and counselling studies (pp. 1458-1459) sets a within-person change in a selected group against figures from other designs. The suggestion that increases in nearly all facets indicate potential improvements in aesthetic and cognitive domains (p. 1459) goes beyond data that contain no aesthetic, creative or cognitive measures. The Discussion does call for replication in larger groups with diverse baseline personalities (p. 1458) and notes that motivation, preparation and spiritual practice may have shaped the result (p. 1459).

timeline.event: Griffiths et al., Study 1 of this analysis: double-blind comparison of psilocybin with methylphenidate in hallucinogen-naive volunteers.
Griffiths et al. (2011), Study 2 of this analysis: four psilocybin doses in ascending or descending order with a placebo session.
Carhart-Harris et al. (2016): LSD in a brain-imaging setting followed by small increases in Openness in healthy volunteers 2 weeks later, as described by Erritzoe et al. (2018, p. 374).
Schmid & Liechti (2018): an LSD study with 1- and 12-month follow-ups did not replicate the Openness increase, as described by Erritzoe et al. (2018, p. 374).

Erritzoe et al.: in an open-label study of psilocybin with psychological support, 19 patients with treatment-resistant depression rose by 4.9 T points in Openness at 3 months, alongside lower Neuroticism and higher Extraversion; no peak-experience factor of the acute experience related to the Openness change, which the authors call somewhat inconsistent with this study.

replication.where_it_stands: Among the sources read for this card, a rise in self-rated Openness after psilocybin was also seen in an open-label study of patients with treatment-resistant depression (Erritzoe et al., 2018), where it was not related to the acute experience; the LSD findings described by Erritzoe et al. (2018) are mixed. Neither psilocybin study had a randomized comparison of personality change or checked it against behaviour or observer ratings. The status is partial because the Openness rise recurred under different conditions while the link to mystical experience did not.

funding.funder: Grants from NIDA (R01DA03889; T32DA007209), the Council on Spiritual Practices, the Heffter Research Institute and the Betsy Gordon Foundation (Funding, p. 1460).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest (p. 1460).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences; Neuroscience); the analysis reuses data from the same group's two trials. Funding is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial that measures personality before and after in both arms (psilocybin against an active placebo of comparable salience), records expectations at baseline, adds ratings by people who know the participant and assessors blind to condition, pre-registers analyses of all five domains, and follows every participant for 12 months or more; repeated in people not selected for spiritual interest or high Openness.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: The estimates on this card (the +2.8 change, the mystical-experience comparison) are changes against each person's own screening score and groups formed by what happened in the session, so the parent studies' randomization does not protect them. Session order was randomized in Study 2 (ascending or descending, with a quasi-randomly placed placebo); this paper does not describe how order was set in Study 1.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: A high dose of psilocybin is recognisable, so blinding to which session held it was probably lost before personality was measured; in Study 2 participants given ascending doses had three lower-dose psilocybin sessions before the high dose, which the authors say could not be isolated (p. 1456); extensive preparation and contact with monitors accompany the drug.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: 52 of 52 at post-test and 51 of 52 at follow-up; two parent-study participants excluded for stated reasons.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-rated personality questionnaires completed by unpaid, motivated, mostly spiritually active volunteers who could probably tell they had received the high dose; expectations and the wish to report change could raise Openness scores, a construct close to describing oneself as open to new experience. No informant ratings.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration mentioned; follow-up reported for subgroups only; five domains and six facets tested without correction; the headline follow-up result sits at p = 0.050.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 is applied as the batch brief directs for MacLean's pooled trials, but the results this card records are within-person pre-post changes and comparisons of groups defined by the session experience, which the parent studies' randomization does not protect. With self-rated outcomes in recognisably treated, highly motivated volunteers, the risk of bias for 'psilocybin increases Openness' is high. The card may be cited for what was observed in this selected sample: an average rise of 2.8 T points in self-rated Openness at 1-2 months, concentrated in those with a complete mystical experience, with wide individual variation and no detectable change in the other four domains; for the 16-month result only with its p value of 0.050 and its restriction to the mystical-experience subgroup; and as hypothesis-generating. It should not be cited as showing that psilocybin or mystical experiences cause lasting personality change, or that behaviour changed.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 52 hallucinogen-naive volunteers (35 from Study 1, 17 from Study 2), mean age 46, 22 men and 30 women (editors' sum); 54% held postgraduate degrees and 90% regularly took part in religious services, discussion groups, prayer or meditation; screening Openness T scores 65.4 and 62.7 against a population mean of 50 (SD 10).

Study conditions: the analysed high-dose session was oral psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg; Study 1 used methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg as active control; Study 2 gave 5, 10, 20 and 30 mg/70 kg in ascending or descending order with a placebo session. Personality (NEO PI-R, T scores) was measured at screening, 1-2 months after each session and about 14 months after the last session.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Psilocybin sessions › Dose conditions; Measures › NEO Personality Inventory

key_findings.finding: Across all 52, Openness rose from screening to 1-2 months after the high-dose session by 2.8 T points (F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023, partial eta squared 0.10); Neuroticism (-0.5, p = 0.62), Extroversion (+0.8, p = 0.38), Agreeableness (+1.7, p = 0.16) and Conscientiousness (-0.9, p = 0.28) did not change significantly; test-retest correlations were 0.61-0.84.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in personality following the psilocybin session, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: within-person standardized change dz about 0.32. For Agreeableness, F(1, 51) = 2.31 corresponds to p = 0.13, not the printed 0.16 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the 30 participants whose first session was placebo, methylphenidate or psilocybin 5 mg/70 kg, Openness did not change after that session (F(1, 29) = 0.52, p = 0.48); this change is not tested against the change after the high-dose session.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in personality following the psilocybin session, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The SOCQ mystical score of the high-dose session (subscale scores spanning 0.03-1.00) correlated with the Openness change (r = 0.42, p = 0.002, n = 52; Spearman 0.47) but not with screening Openness (r = 0.12, p = 0.41). Openness change also correlated with the Mysticism Scale (r = 0.33), OSE (0.44), VUS, the visionary-restructuralization scale (0.41), and AIA, the dread-of-ego-dissolution scale (0.31); the SOCQ added R-squared 0.042 to 0.12 beyond each.
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship between session-day effects and changes in Openness, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 (p. 1457)
key_findings.note: Editors' 95% CI for r = 0.42 with n = 52: about 0.17 to 0.62 (Fisher z).

key_findings.finding: 30 of 52 met the criterion for a complete mystical experience. Time by group interaction F(1, 50) = 9.32, p = 0.004, partial eta squared 0.16: Openness +5.7 in the complete group (t(29) = 3.44, p = 0.002) and -1.2 in the others (t(21) = 0.87, p = 0.39). Five of six facets (Fantasy, Aesthetics, Feelings, Ideas, Values; not Actions) showed the same interaction (p 0.010-0.038).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effect of mystical experience on changes in Openness, 1st paragraph; Figures 2 and 3 (p. 1458)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: dz about 0.63 in the complete group. The groups are defined by the session experience, not by randomization.

key_findings.finding: At follow-up, a mean of 16 months after the high-dose session, the complete-mystical group's Openness was slightly lower than at post-test (difference p = 0.12) and 4.2 T points above screening (F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050, partial eta squared 0.13); the other group (n = 21) was 0.3 below screening (p = 0.86). The whole-sample follow-up change is not reported.
key_findings.note: F(1, 29) = 4.17 corresponds to p = 0.0503 (editors' calculation). Editors' weighted mean of the two subgroups: about +2.3 T points for all 51, untested.

key_findings.finding: In the editors' reading of Figure 1, individual changes from screening to post-test ranged from about -12 to about +36 T points; about 17 of the 51 visible points lie below zero (lower Openness after the session), and the three largest increases (about +21, +26 and +36) were at high mystical scores.
key_findings.note: Read by the editors from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1 (approximate; 51 of 52 points visible, one presumably overlapping). Without the three largest changes the mean change of the other 49 would be about +1.3 T points (editors' approximate calculation, (2.8 x 52 - 83)/49).

key_findings.finding: The overall pattern was similar in Study 1 and Study 2 (complete-group Openness change between studies p = 0.11), and counting three Study 2 participants whose complete mystical experience came at 20 mg/70 kg rather than 30 mg/70 kg (complete group n = 33) did not change the results.

The authors compare the rise of more than 4 T points from screening to follow-up in the complete-mystical group with the usual decline of Openness of about 1 T point per decade in normal ageing and with smaller increases reported after successful antidepressant treatment and intensive outpatient counselling; these comparison figures come from other studies (Terracciano et al., 2005; Costa et al., 2005; Piedmont, 2001).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1458, right column, continuing on p. 1459)

key_findings.finding: The authors contrast their result with a controlled LSD study (McGlothlin et al., 1967) that found no significant improvement in creativity or aesthetic measures at 6 months, writing that differences in participants' motivation and preparation (paid graduate students with little interest in LSD and minimal support there, unpaid motivated volunteers with extensive preparation here) likely contributed to the different long-term outcomes, and that it is possible that spiritually active people are particularly sensitive to the mystical-type effects that predicted the Openness increase.

reporting_issues.issue: The follow-up result for the complete-mystical group is reported as significantly higher than screening at F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050; that F corresponds to p = 0.0503 (editors' calculation), at or just above the 0.05 threshold. The abstract, Results and Discussion all describe it as significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that the Openness increase lasted more than a year rests on a borderline result in a subgroup of 30.

reporting_issues.issue: The whole-sample Openness change at follow-up is not reported; only the two mystical-experience subgroups are (+4.2 and -0.3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the average participant's Openness was still higher after about 16 months is unknown; the editors' weighted estimate (about +2.3) is untested.

reporting_issues.issue: The specificity of the change to psilocybin rests on two separate within-group tests (p = 0.023 after the high-dose session; p = 0.48 after a first session without it); the difference between the two changes is not tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: A significant change in one condition and a non-significant change in another do not show that the two differ; the evidence that psilocybin, rather than time or retesting, produced the change is indirect.

reporting_issues.issue: For Agreeableness, F(1, 51) = 2.31 is printed with p = 0.16; that F corresponds to p = 0.13 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the conclusion of no significant change is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: No check of the robustness of the mean change is reported, although Figure 1 shows three increases of about 21, 26 and 36 T points (read from the figure) in a sample whose mean change is 2.8; the correlations were confirmed with Spearman coefficients, but the ANOVA results were not.
reporting_issues.consequence: The average rise may depend substantially on a few participants (the editors' approximate recalculation without them gives about +1.3); its size is less certain than the printed statistics suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'no complete mystical experience' group has 22 participants at post-test and 21 at follow-up; the missing participant is not mentioned.

disagreements.first_pass: The authors contrast their result with a controlled LSD study (McGlothlin et al., 1967) that found no lasting change in creativity or aesthetic measures at 6 months, attributing the difference to participants' motivation and preparation (paid graduate students with little interest in LSD and minimal support there, unpaid motivated volunteers with extensive preparation here), and suggest that spiritually active people may be especially sensitive to the mystical-type effects that predicted the Openness increase.
disagreements.reviewer: The authors contrast their result with a controlled LSD study (McGlothlin et al., 1967) that found no significant improvement in creativity or aesthetic measures at 6 months, writing that differences in participants' motivation and preparation (paid graduate students with little interest in LSD and minimal support there, unpaid motivated volunteers with extensive preparation here) likely contributed to the different long-term outcomes, and that it is possible that spiritually active people are particularly sensitive to the mystical-type effects that predicted the Openness increase.
disagreements.resolution: Second reader's correction adopted by the AI co-editor (AI reader 687 (round-2 check))

disagreements.reviewer: The parent Study 1 (Griffiths et al., 2006, p. 278; its PDF is now on file) reported that no NEO PI-R factor was differentially affected by psilocybin: the randomized order groups (15 and 15) did not differ significantly 2 months after session 1, and the methylphenidate-first group showed no significant change after its psilocybin session. This is the only randomized comparison of personality change in these data, and it was null (small groups, no values shown); cannot_establish and comparison should mention it.
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.

disagreements.reviewer: At least five of the 35 Study 1 participants were decoy-arm volunteers of Griffiths et al. (2006), whose third, psilocybin session was unblinded (Griffiths 2006, pp. 269, 271), while this paper describes the high-dose session as blind to timing for all (an inference by the editors); relevant to RoB domain 2.
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.
